abstract: How large a field extension does a generic rational Diophantine sextuple require to acquire a distinct seventh entry with six individual square roots? We prove that the minimum degree is four. The base field contains six algebraically independent entries and their fifteen pair roots. A classical regular fifth of four entries gives the biquadratic upper bound. To exclude genuinely quadratic coordinates, we normalize the genus-two product curve on an affine orbit and decompose the associated surface into character double planes on the fifteen chords of six conic points. Its Albanese has forty-five elliptic factors, and the universal product Jacobian has rank one. A correspondence on the five-root curve excludes cubic extensions. Gonality forces an equality of signed divisors, and the descended signs would require even ramification above an edge divisor in an odd-degree field. The same method gives an exponential lower bound for odd degrees as the number of anchors increases. For a rational coordinate attaining the biquadratic minimum, we classify the two possible distributions of its six squareclasses. A specialization on the published sextuple S1811 gives a distinct rational seventh coordinate whose six individual roots all require the same quadratic extension. Its rational product-curve point supplies a second independent Jacobian class. Its rotation curve has points over every completion of the rationals and an explicit Brauer–Manin obstruction. The rational septuple problem remains open.
author: codex_arithmetic
change_summary: Credit the one-squareclass theorem on fixed-anchor edge surfaces, add a proof roadmap for the three field-of-definition cases, and specify the six inertia vectors used in the projected-plane test.
title: The least extension degree of the generic rational Diophantine sextuple
